title: What artificial intelligence includes
summary: A map of AI before the vocabulary gets in the way: reasoning, learning, perception, generation, and action.
html:
A map of AI before the vocabulary gets in the way: reasoning, learning, perception, generation, and action.

How the pieces connect

Start with the task

Artificial intelligence studies systems that perform tasks involving perception, reasoning, learning, or decision-making. A system can search a game tree without learning anything. A classifier can learn from labeled examples without generating text. A language model can generate fluent text without checking whether its claims are true. These are different capabilities and need different tests.

The nested families

Machine learning is one approach to AI: fit behavior from data. Deep learning uses layered neural networks to learn representations. Generative models learn to produce samples such as text, images, audio, or molecular structures. An agent combines a policy or model with observations, tools, and an environment in which actions have consequences. These categories overlap; they do not form a leaderboard.

Training and inference

Training changes learned parameters using an objective and data. Inference applies a trained system to new inputs. A prompt usually changes the input context, not the model weights. Retrieval supplies external information. Fine-tuning updates parameters. A production application may use all four and must track which component caused a result.

What to learn first

Understand how computers represent and move data, then the mathematics of vectors, uncertainty, and gradients. Learn a small supervised learning pipeline before studying transformers. After that, choose a branch: build applications, train models, optimize hardware, study multimodal systems, or evaluate risks. Each branch builds on the same shared foundations.

Worked example

ProblemCandidate approachUseful test
Find a routeGraph searchPath cost and constraints
Predict equipment failureSupervised learningRecall at an acceptable false-alarm rate
Answer a policy questionRetrieval plus generationEvidence support and abstention
Control a robotPerception, planning, controlTask success and physical constraint violations

What goes wrong

Treating “AI” as synonymous with a chatbot hides the engineering choices. A deterministic rule can be more suitable than a learned model when the desired behavior is known exactly.

Check your understanding

Does adding a document to an LLM prompt train the model?

Reveal the explanation

No. It conditions this inference request. A training step requires a learning objective and a parameter update.

An operating model for what artificial intelligence includes

The first design decision is not “which model?” It is whether the task needs a learned approximation at all. A rule, database query, calculator, optimizer, retrieval system, classifier, and generative model each fail in different ways. The most useful AI systems make those boundaries visible rather than pretending one component can do every job.

The gotcha. A clean workflow diagram describes dependency order. It does not prove that any boundary is correct; each transition needs its own observable acceptance test.

Worked system: choose the smallest component that owns the decision

A support portal receives a question about a customer’s current invoice. A language model can explain the result, but it should not invent the amount. The correct path is a database query for the authoritative balance, a calculator for deterministic arithmetic, retrieval for the applicable policy text, and a generative component only for the explanation. Each tool has a distinct contract and failure mode; combining them into “ask the model” hides those boundaries.

Start by naming the input, intended decision, source of truth, acceptable abstention, and cost of a harmful error. Then choose the smallest component that can own each part. This is the core architectural move in AI systems: models are useful approximators, while identity, permissions, records, arithmetic, and irreversible actions usually belong to components with explicit guarantees.

Five lenses for reading any AI claim

Capability. What behavior was demonstrated, on what task, and under which conditions? A benchmark score and a compelling demo answer a limited capability question; they do not prove the system can operate reliably in an open workflow. System. What data, memory, retrieval, tools, evaluators, and human interventions make the behavior possible? A model is one component inside a larger causal chain. Reliability. What happens at the edge: rare inputs, long sequences, missing evidence, distribution shifts, malicious text, or a failing dependency? Product quality is usually dominated by these paths rather than the median example.

Economics and infrastructure. What hardware, energy, capital, organization, and supply chain are required for the claimed capability to exist at scale? A feature that works in a controlled demo can face an entirely different constraint when multiplied across millions of requests. Power and legitimacy. Who supplies the data, owns the infrastructure, absorbs errors, and has a route to contest a decision? This is not an ethical afterthought. It shapes which objectives are optimized, which failures are visible, and which systems are permitted to operate.

The Perspective volume applies these lenses to the people, fault lines, physical constraints, and prediction record surrounding AI. The technical library explains how systems work; the perspective work asks what their builders believe, what evidence would change a view, and what the system is actually allowed to decide. Keeping both in one field library makes it harder to confuse capability with inevitability.

Notebook: Trace a byte budget

Write an acceptance test before choosing a model. For each intended action, define the available evidence, an acceptable abstention path, the human or system allowed to act, and what counts as a harmful error.

items = 1_000_000
bytes_per_item = 4
working_set = items * bytes_per_item
print(f"{working_set / 2**20:.1f} MiB")
# Now include every copy, index, and temporary buffer.
What to test next. 1. Frame the task: State the input, output, decision, and cost of failure. 2. Choose a capability: Search, prediction, generation, perception, or control. 3. Test the behavior: Use evidence that matches the intended use. 4. Operate the system: Monitor exceptions, feedback, and changing conditions.

The gotcha. A small inspection script proves only the quantities it prints. Preserve units, shapes, versions, and the input fixture beside its output.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Frame the task. State the input, output, decision, and cost of failure.
  2. Choose a capability. Search, prediction, generation, perception, or control.
  3. Test the behavior. Use evidence that matches the intended use.
  4. Operate the system. Monitor exceptions, feedback, and changing conditions.

Write an acceptance test before choosing a model. For each intended action, define the available evidence, an acceptable abstention path, the human or system allowed to act, and what counts as a harmful error.

The gotcha. Passing each component check separately does not prove the composed path preserves identity, units, ordering, or authority.

Capability is only one layer of an AI system

A model converts an input representation into an output representation. A useful system must also decide what information enters that model, what authority follows from its output, and how failures become visible. Treating the model as the entire product hides the parts that usually determine reliability.

  • Capability layer. Test whether the learned component can classify, rank, retrieve, generate, perceive, plan, or control under a stated distribution. A successful demonstration establishes possibility. It does not establish a stable failure rate.
  • System layer. Trace acquisition, preprocessing, model execution, retrieval, tools, storage, authentication, interface, and monitoring. Each boundary can corrupt meaning even when every component returns a technically valid result.
  • Decision layer. Define who or what acts on the output. A recommendation shown to an analyst has a different risk boundary from an automatic payment, code deployment, medical escalation, or physical motion.
  • Evidence layer. Match evidence to the claim. Unit tests support implementation claims. Held-out evaluations support behavioral claims. Controlled experiments support causal claims. Field operation supports reliability and economic claims.

The gotcha. Teams often improve model quality while the product remains unchanged because the binding constraint sits in retrieval, workflow integration, latency, permissions, or user trust.

Five lenses for reading any AI claim

  • Capability. Ask exactly what input produced what output, under which tools, prompt, sampling settings, time budget, and human assistance.
  • Reliability. Ask for the denominator: how many trials, which failures, what variance across seeds and subgroups, and how the system handles an unsupported request.
  • Infrastructure. Count memory, compute, network traffic, data movement, queueing, and service dependencies. A model that fits on one accelerator may still need a distributed serving system to meet demand.
  • Economics. Compare cost per accepted task at equal quality. Include retries, review, retrieval, storage, network transfer, idle capacity, and incidents.
  • Power. Identify who controls data, compute, distribution, labor, standards, and the right to challenge a decision. Technical capability does not determine how benefits and costs are allocated.

The gotcha. A benchmark result can be correct and still fail to support the much larger social or commercial claim attached to it.

From task statement to operating system

A disciplined AI project begins with an observable decision rather than a model family. Write down the input available at decision time, the output contract, the actor who consumes it, the cost of each error, and the fallback when evidence is missing. This turns a vague wish for intelligence into an engineering boundary.

  • Rules and programs. Use deterministic logic when the world is closed, the rules can be stated, and violations must fail hard. Tax calculations, schema checks, access control, and protocol parsing belong here.
  • Search and optimization. Use an explicit objective and constraints when the system must choose among alternatives. Route planning, scheduling, resource allocation, and satisfiability can often provide checkable solutions.
  • Statistical prediction. Use learned models when patterns must be inferred from examples and uncertainty is expected. Define the target population and loss before selecting the estimator.
  • Retrieval. Use indexes when the answer already exists in a corpus and provenance matters. A generator can express retrieved evidence, but it should not replace the retrieval test.
  • Generation. Use generative models when the output space is too open to enumerate. Constrain format, ground claims, and keep consequential actions behind explicit authorization.

The gotcha. Selecting a general model first encourages the project to absorb tasks that a database, calculator, or verifier could perform more cheaply and reliably.

The lifecycle changes the system after launch

Training freezes one relationship between data, parameters, and objective. Deployment introduces users, incentives, new distributions, and feedback. The deployed system can change its own future inputs: recommendations affect clicks, moderation affects what is posted, and automated decisions affect who appears in later training data.

  • Data generation. Record how examples entered the dataset, who was excluded, when labels became available, and which policy created the observed behavior.
  • Evaluation. Protect a held-out set from model selection. Add slices, counterexamples, adversarial cases, latency, cost, and calibration that reflect the operating decision.
  • Release. Version weights, tokenizer, prompts, preprocessing, retrieval index, tool policy, and runtime as one compatible artifact set. A model-only rollback can preserve the incident.
  • Monitoring. Measure input drift, outcome drift, abstention, tool authorization, queue time, and user-impacting failure. Logs should minimize sensitive content while retaining enough causal structure for diagnosis.
  • Retirement. Define how a model, index, or dataset stops serving, how dependent systems migrate, and how retained data is deleted or archived.

The gotcha. Feedback collected from a deployed policy is selected by that policy. Treating it as an unbiased sample can reinforce mistakes while dashboards appear to improve.

The field is a stack of contracts

LayerPrimary contractTypical evidenceCharacteristic failure
HardwareExecute supported operations within capacityKernel correctness, bytes, latency, energyBandwidth or memory ceiling
NumericsApproximate mathematical operations within toleranceError bounds, finite checks, conditioningOverflow, underflow, cancellation
ModelMap a defined input distribution to useful outputsHeld-out tasks, slices, calibrationShift, shortcut, confabulation
ApplicationAssemble evidence, tools, and permissionsEnd-to-end tests and tracesWrong context or excess authority
OrganizationAssign ownership, review, and incident responseRunbooks, audits, field outcomesNo accountable decision owner
SocietyAllocate benefits, costs, and recourseDistributional and institutional evidenceConcentrated power or unchallengeable harm

The gotcha. Success at one layer cannot certify the layer above it. Correct matrix multiplication does not prove a useful model; a useful model does not prove a legitimate decision.
